title: Modha Rathri
verdict: Hmm... One wedding night. A whole village on trial.
dek: A wedding-night comedy that exposes the village's old thinking. The people are interesting, even when the shouting becomes exhausting.
review: The title makes you expect a wedding-night comedy. Modha Rathri is interested in something larger: how a village can turn two people's private lives into everybody's business.

Marudhu and Muthuchelvi enter a marriage neither seems fully prepared to embrace. Their disappearance creates suspicion, gossip, arguments and family panic. The resulting confusion becomes the film's central comic engine.

The most interesting people are not necessarily the newlyweds. It is the adults surrounding them, carrying rules about masculinity, reputation and obedience that collapse whenever common sense becomes necessary.
Rishikanth's Marudhu works because he does not constantly try to dominate the screen. His restrained reactions provide balance when the supporting characters become louder.

Anishma Anilkumar gives Muthuchelvi emotional weight. Her character carries the expectations surrounding marriage and the consequences of decisions that other people believe they have a right to make.
The relationship becomes more meaningful when the film allows these two people to understand each other instead of manufacturing another misunderstanding.

Director Raja Karuppasamy uses the wedding to question old social habits. The families appear deeply concerned about public reputation, but considerably less interested in whether the individuals involved are comfortable.

The film's observations about patriarchy, gender expectations and social embarrassment are more valuable than its most exaggerated jokes. Its humour works best when ordinary behaviour exposes extraordinary hypocrisy.
But the comedy eventually becomes overcrowded. Too many characters shout, panic and repeat accusations. A few carefully timed silences could have generated more laughter than another argument.
Some developments also become predictable. Once the audience understands a misunderstanding, prolonging it requires new character insight rather than simply introducing more confusion.
Bharath Sankar's music and the rural atmosphere give the film a distinctive identity. The ensemble makes the village feel inhabited rather than constructed merely for jokes.
Raja Karuppasamy deserves credit for attempting comedy with a human argument underneath it. He wants us to examine who controls marriage decisions and why families confuse authority with affection.
The execution is uneven, particularly when comic noise overwhelms the emotional journey. Still, the film has more to offer than the expectations created by its provocative title.
Modha Rathri is better when it trusts its characters than when it manufactures another round of chaos. Not every joke lands, but the story has something worthwhile underneath the noise.
works: Rishikanth's restraint, Anishma Anilkumar's emotional presence, rural atmosphere, social observations, ensemble performances and situational humour.
misses: Overcrowded comedy, repetitive shouting, predictable developments and uneven pacing.
